![](images/e2/e25e66141569f5324759eb15a1dcf8b143f5018cf35e957f7a212ba3b45b3556.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186315028 :question/worked-solution "If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,5),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,5), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-5,0).\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-(3(-x)^{2}-2(-x)) \\  & =-(3{x}^{2}+2x) \\  & =-3{x}^{2}-2x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186379568 :question/worked-solution "If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-\pi ,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-((-x)^{2}+4(-x)-9) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-4x-9) \\  & =-{x}^{2}+4x+9.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186379582 :question/problem "$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=-4$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier sine series of the **odd** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${b}_{n}.$

$\,{b}_{n}=$ {{field-1}}" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167284 :question/problem "$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=2$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier sine series of the **odd** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${b}_{n}.$

$\,{b}_{n}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=2$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{4}{n\pi }[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-\frac{4}{n\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{4(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ))}{n\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{4(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi n}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164929 :answer-field/correct "answer-d703d305-1fef-58e0-ac9f-aedced6da080" :answer-field/choices ["answer-319ba16a-7d74-5bcd-99b2-bc9850751276" "answer-7a9fb755-7be5-5ae8-be1c-cea88ce12977" "answer-0288041e-13a5-5541-bbd8-c13988faf24e" "answer-82973565-ede8-565e-a9ef-215aaa0446b5" "answer-d703d305-1fef-58e0-ac9f-aedced6da080"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-319ba16a-7d74-5bcd-99b2-bc9850751276" :answer/id #uuid "319ba16a-7d74-5bcd-99b2-bc9850751276" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{(1-(-1)^{n})}{4\pi n}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7a9fb755-7be5-5ae8-be1c-cea88ce12977" :answer/id #uuid "7a9fb755-7be5-5ae8-be1c-cea88ce12977" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2(1+(-1)^{n})}{\pi n}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0288041e-13a5-5541-bbd8-c13988faf24e" :answer/id #uuid "0288041e-13a5-5541-bbd8-c13988faf24e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi n}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-82973565-ede8-565e-a9ef-215aaa0446b5" :answer/id #uuid "82973565-ede8-565e-a9ef-215aaa0446b5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4(1+(-1)^{n})}{\pi n}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d703d305-1fef-58e0-ac9f-aedced6da080" :answer/id #uuid "d703d305-1fef-58e0-ac9f-aedced6da080" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi n}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168039 :tutorial/content "In the earlier topics, we saw that *symmetry* can force many Fourier coefficients to be zero automatically.
In particular, if a $2\pi$-periodic function is *odd*, then its Fourier series has *sine terms only*.

A **Fourier sine series** uses this idea when a function is initially given only on the half-interval, say, $[0,\pi),$ but we want a full Fourier series on $[-\pi,\pi)$ (and then a $2\pi$-periodic extension to all real $x$).

To do this, we start with a function $F(x)$ on $[0,\pi)$ and define its **odd extension** $f(x)$ to $(-\pi,\pi)$ by
![](images/77/776119c1d430a7d50051ae0e00e254f9d22782bc192aa8a0cab9cc227fe460db.svg)

For example, a function $F(x),$ defined on $x \in [0,1),$ and its odd extension $f(x)$ to $x \in (-1,1)$ are shown below.

![](images/2f/2f915ed450be1abf672e3fd86b56c02820514a778a4d4d174409f5bd99da6834.png)

By construction, $f$ is an *odd* function, meaning $f(-x)=-f(x)$. Because $f$ is odd, its Fourier series on $[-\pi,\pi)$ has *sine terms only*:

$$
f(x)\sim \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\sin(nx)
$$

Since $f(x)$ is odd and $\sin(nx)$ is odd for any $n \geq 1,$ then $f(x)\sin(nx)$ must be even.
So, the sine coefficients can be computed using the *half-range formula*:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot 2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

So in practice, the workflow is the following:

1\. Start with $F$ on $[0,\pi)$ and form the odd extension $f$ on $(-\pi,\pi).$

2\. Compute $b_n$ from the half-range integral on $[0,\pi).$

3\. Write the Fourier sine series of $f.$

Let's see some concrete examples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166991 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$
b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=4x$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
b_n = \dfrac{8}{\pi}\int_0^\pi x \sin(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{8}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{8}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{8}{n\pi }(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =-\frac{8\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have

$$
b_n = -\dfrac{8(-1)^n}{n}=\dfrac{8(-1)^{n+1}}{n}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{8(-1)^{n+1}}{n} \cdot \sin(nx).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050730} {:db/id 17592186050929} {:db/id 17592186167283 :question/id #uuid "37a89f3d-e2cd-5d21-bb53-6d99da952356" :question/math-academy-id "q-340629"} {:db/id 17592186167284 :question/id #uuid "7a38bbe2-8cc7-5da0-8136-af259e1c0160" :question/math-academy-id "q-340708" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166956 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1a85c9c4-8563-55e0-9d4f-7d61d3be6243" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Sine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c73bb553-e1ce-5193-92b0-6d152c45f847" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(4(1 + (-1)^{n}))/(πn)" :db/id 17592186164930} {:answer/id #uuid "dfe83b98-8c7b-5459-8d63-b30d9d1018e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(2(1 + (-1)^{n}))/(πn)" :db/id 17592186164931} {:answer/id #uuid "0d1fb54f-7ffb-58b0-98e3-bd8b42137fb7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(4(1 - (-1)^{n}))/(πn)" :db/id 17592186164932} {:answer/id #uuid "3bc0f9c9-267c-5853-a013-743020911216" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(2(1 - (-1)^{n}))/(πn)" :db/id 17592186164933} {:answer/id #uuid "5a6d7840-62a9-5cb3-8276-7b1f3e379232" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "((1 - (-1)^{n}))/(4πn)" :db/id 17592186164934}] :answer-field/id #uuid "32a95669-d006-58f5-a342-6964952c273c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494 :db/ident :answer-field.type/select} :db/id 17592186164929}] :question/problem "$f(x)∼∑_(n = 1)^(∞)b_{n}\sin (nx)$

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167931 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168039 :tutorial/content "In the earlier topics, we saw that *symmetry* can force many Fourier coefficients to be zero automatically.
In particular, if a $2\pi$-periodic function is *odd*, then its Fourier series has *sine terms only*.

A **Fourier sine series** uses this idea when a function is initially given only on the half-interval, say, $[0,\pi),$ but we want a full Fourier series on $[-\pi,\pi)$ (and then a $2\pi$-periodic extension to all real $x$).

Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization.
